title: Invalidate cached block metadata when the backing file is recreated
applies_when: A file-backed or mmap cache restores cached-block metadata after restart, unpickling or reopening, and its named backing file may have been deleted. The block set may be shared with caller bookkeeping.
lesson: A saved path and cached-block set do not prove that the corresponding bytes still exist. When creating a new backing file, invalidate the old block metadata before treating any block as a hit; otherwise a new zero-filled mapping can return plausible but wrong bytes without calling the fetcher. Preserve caller aliases by clearing a shared mutable set in place rather than replacing it. Compare a deleted-backing-file case against an existing-file reuse control, and assert both returned bytes and fetcher calls. Test the actual public reopening path as well as serialization, because a synthetic cache constructor alone can miss producer/consumer bookkeeping.
avoid_when: Do not invalidate an existing valid file on every open or discard unrelated cached data. Cross-process writers, persisted metadata merges, content changes under an unchanged path and generation/version protocols need separate contracts. The fsspec evidence below establishes missing-file cache validity and alias preservation only; it does not fix serialization of an HTTP-bound asynchronous fetcher, prove all CachingFileSystem recovery paths, or establish performance or maintainer acceptance.

evidence.note: Proposed, unmerged missing named mmap backing-file fix. Four native regressions/controls fail 3 and pass 1 on the unchanged source, then all pass; the public HTTP reader reopening case reaches the same bug. Separate native Windows mmap/pickle controls confirm the file-backed mechanism. This is scoped correctness evidence, not full CI or maintainer acceptance.

Exact proposed tests preserve the existing-file no-refetch control, verify clearing the caller-shared set without changing its identity, and reopen a real loopback HTTP reader after removing the backing file.
